pages.title: Aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular events

claims.text: In six primary prevention trials of about 95,000 individuals at low average risk, aspirin allocation produced a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001), driven mainly by a reduction of about a fifth in non-fatal myocardial infarction.

evidence.quote: In the primary prevention trials, aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001), due mainly to a reduction of about a fifth in non-fatal myocardial infarction (0.18%vs 0.23% per year, p<0.0001).

claims.text: In a meta-analysis of 13 trials randomizing 164,225 participants without known cardiovascular disease, aspirin use was associated with a significant reduction in the composite cardiovascular outcome compared with no aspirin (57.1 vs 61.4 per 10,000 participant-years; HR 0.89, 95% credible interval 0.84-0.95; absolute risk reduction 0.38%, number needed to treat 265).

evidence.quote: Aspirin use was associated with significant reductions in the composite cardiovascular outcome compared with no aspirin (57.1 per 10 000 participant-years with aspirin and 61.4 per 10 000 participant-years with no aspirin) (hazard ratio [HR], 0.89 [95% credible interval, 0.84-0.95]; absolute risk reduction, 0.38% [95% CI, 0.20%-0.55%]; number needed to treat, 265).

claims.text: In the ARRIVE trial of 12,546 patients at moderate estimated risk, the primary composite endpoint occurred in 269 (4.29%) patients on aspirin versus 281 (4.48%) on placebo, a non-significant difference (HR 0.96; 95% CI 0.81-1.13; p=0.6038).

evidence.quote: In the intention-to-treat analysis, the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038).

claims.text: In the Japanese Primary Prevention Project of 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with atherosclerotic risk factors, the 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate did not differ significantly between aspirin and no aspirin (2.77% vs 2.96%; HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.77-1.15; P=.54).

evidence.quote: The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups (2.77% [95% CI, 2.40%-3.20%] for aspirin vs 2.96% [95% CI, 2.58%-3.40%] for no aspirin; hazard ratio [HR], 0.94 [95% CI, 0.77-1.15]; P = .54).

claims.text: In ASPREE, among 19,114 older adults without cardiovascular disease, the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years with aspirin and 11.3 with placebo, a non-significant difference (HR 0.95; 95% CI 0.83-1.08).

evidence.quote: After a median of 4.7 years of follow-up, the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.3 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.08).

claims.text: In the ASCEND trial of 15,480 adults with diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease, serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of the aspirin group than the placebo group (658 participants [8.5%] vs 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.79-0.97; P=0.01).

evidence.quote: During a mean follow-up of 7.4 years, serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of participants in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (658 participants [8.5%] vs. 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio, 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79 to 0.97; P=0.01).

claims.text: Across the primary prevention trials, aspirin's effect on stroke was not significant (0.20% vs 0.21% per year, p=0.4) and vascular mortality did not differ significantly (0.19% vs 0.19% per year, p=0.7).

evidence.quote: The net effect on stroke was not significant (0.20%vs 0.21% per year, p=0.4: haemorrhagic stroke 0.04%vs 0.03%, p=0.05; other stroke 0.16%vs 0.18% per year, p=0.08). Vascular mortality did not differ significantly (0.19%vs 0.19% per year, p=0.7).

claims.text: In the primary prevention trials, aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10% vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001).

evidence.quote: Aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10%vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001), and the main risk factors for coronary disease were also risk factors for bleeding.

claims.text: In the meta-analysis of 13 trials, aspirin use was associated with an increased risk of major bleeding compared with no aspirin (23.1 vs 16.4 per 10,000 participant-years; HR 1.43, 95% credible interval 1.30-1.56; absolute risk increase 0.47%; number needed to harm 210).

evidence.quote: Aspirin use was associated with an increased risk of major bleeding events compared with no aspirin (23.1 per 10 000 participant-years with aspirin and 16.4 per 10 000 participant-years with no aspirin) (HR, 1.43 [95% credible interval, 1.30-1.56]; absolute risk increase, 0.47% [95% CI, 0.34%-0.62%]; number needed to harm, 210).

claims.text: In ARRIVE, gastrointestinal bleeding events (mostly mild) occurred in 61 (0.97%) patients on aspirin versus 29 (0.46%) on placebo (HR 2.11; 95% CI 1.36-3.28; p=0.0007).

evidence.quote: Gastrointestinal bleeding events (mostly mild) occurred in 61 (0·97%) patients in the aspirin group versus 29 (0·46%) in the placebo group (HR 2·11; 95% CI 1·36-3·28; p=0·0007).

claims.text: In ASCEND, major bleeding events occurred in 314 participants (4.1%) on aspirin versus 245 (3.2%) on placebo (rate ratio 1.29; 95% CI 1.09-1.52; P=0.003), with most of the excess being gastrointestinal and other extracranial bleeding.

evidence.quote: In contrast, major bleeding events occurred in 314 participants (4.1%) in the aspirin group, as compared with 245 (3.2%) in the placebo group (rate ratio, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.09 to 1.52; P=0.003), with most of the excess being gastrointestinal bleeding and other extracranial bleeding.

claims.text: In ASPREE, the rate of major hemorrhage was 8.6 events per 1000 person-years with aspirin and 6.2 with placebo (HR 1.38; 95% CI 1.18-1.62; P<0.001).

evidence.quote: The rate of major hemorrhage was 8.6 events per 1000 person-years and 6.2 events per 1000 person-years, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.18 to 1.62; P<0.001).

claims.text: In primary prevention without previous disease, aspirin is of uncertain net value because the reduction in occlusive events must be weighed against any increase in major bleeds.

evidence.quote: In primary prevention without previous disease, aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds.

claims.text: In ASCEND, aspirin prevented serious vascular events in persons with diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease but also caused major bleeding events, and the absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard.

evidence.quote: Aspirin use prevented serious vascular events in persons who had diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at trial entry, but it also caused major bleeding events. The absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard.

claims.text: The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for primary prevention in adults aged 40 to 59 years with a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit, and that initiating aspirin in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit.

evidence.quote: The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit. The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit.

claims.text: The USPSTF recommends that the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin for primary prevention in adults aged 40 to 59 years with a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk be individual, and recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin in adults 60 years or older.

evidence.quote: The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one. Evidence indicates that the net benefit of aspirin use in this group is small. Persons who are not at increased risk for bleeding and are willing to take low-dose aspirin daily are more likely to benefit. (C recommendation) The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation).

pages.title: Meta-analysis of aspirin for primary prevention (JAMA 2019)

claims.text: This systematic review and meta-analysis included 13 randomized trials enrolling at least 1000 participants with no known cardiovascular disease and at least 12 months of follow-up, randomizing 164,225 participants with 1,050,511 participant-years of follow-up.

evidence.quote: Randomized clinical trials enrolling at least 1000 participants with no known cardiovascular disease and a follow-up of at least 12 months were included.
A total of 13 trials randomizing 164 225 participants with 1 050 511 participant-years of follow-up were included.

claims.text: The median age of trial participants was 62 years (range 53-74), 47% were men, 19% had diabetes, and the median baseline risk of the primary cardiovascular outcome was 9.2% (range 2.6%-15.9%).

evidence.quote: The median age of trial participants was 62 years (range, 53-74), 77 501 (47%) were men, 30 361 (19%) had diabetes, and the median baseline risk of the primary cardiovascular outcome was 9.2% (range, 2.6%-15.9%).

claims.text: Aspirin use was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding in individuals without cardiovascular disease.

evidence.quote: The use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding.

pages.title: US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation on aspirin use to prevent cardiovascular disease (2022)

claims.text: The 2022 USPSTF recommendation applies to adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD who are not at increased risk for bleeding.

evidence.quote: Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding (eg, no history of gastrointestinal ulcers, recent bleeding, other medical conditions, or use of medications that increase bleeding risk).

claims.text: The USPSTF commissioned a systematic review on the effectiveness of aspirin to reduce CVD events, cardiovascular mortality and all-cause mortality in persons without a history of CVD, and a microsimulation modeling study of the net balance of benefits and harms stratified by age, sex and CVD risk level.

evidence.quote: To update its 2016 recommendation, the US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) commissioned a systematic review on the effectiveness of aspirin to reduce the risk of CVD events (myocardial infarction and stroke), cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality in persons without a history of CVD.

The USPSTF also commissioned a microsimulation modeling study to assess the net balance of benefits and harms from aspirin use for primary prevention of CVD and CRC, stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level.

claims.text: ARRIVE was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study in seven countries that enrolled patients aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older with moderate estimated cardiovascular risk, excluding those at high bleeding risk or with diabetes.

evidence.quote: ARRIVE is a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study done in seven countries. Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors. We excluded patients at high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or other bleeding, or diabetes.

claims.text: Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12,546 patients were enrolled at 501 study sites and randomly assigned to aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276), with a median follow-up of 60 months.

evidence.quote: Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites. Median follow-up was 60 months.

claims.text: The overall incidence of serious adverse events was similar in both treatment groups (1266 [20.19%] with aspirin vs 1311 [20.89%] with placebo), as was the overall incidence of adverse events (5142 [82.01%] vs 5129 [81.72%]).

evidence.quote: The overall incidence rate of serious adverse events was similar in both treatment groups (n=1266 [20·19%] in the aspirin group vs n=1311 [20·89%] in the placebo group. The overall incidence of adverse events was similar in both treatment groups (n=5142 [82·01%] vs n=5129 [81·72%] in the placebo group).

claims.text: There were 321 documented deaths in the intention-to-treat population (160 [2.55%] with aspirin vs 161 [2.57%] with placebo).

evidence.quote: There were 321 documented deaths in the intention-to-treat population (n=160 [2·55%] vs n=161 [2·57%] of 6276 patients in the placebo group).

claims.text: ASCEND randomly assigned adults with diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease to aspirin 100 mg daily or matching placebo, with a primary efficacy outcome of first serious vascular event and a primary safety outcome of first major bleeding event.

evidence.quote: We randomly assigned adults who had diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease to receive aspirin at a dose of 100 mg daily or matching placebo. The primary efficacy outcome was the first serious vascular event (i.e., myocardial infarction, stroke or transient ischemic attack, or death from any vascular cause, excluding any confirmed intracranial hemorrhage). The primary safety outcome was the first major bleeding event (i.e., intracranial hemorrhage, sight-threatening bleeding event in the eye, gastrointestinal bleeding, or other serious bleeding).

claims.text: A total of 15,480 participants underwent randomization, with a mean follow-up of 7.4 years.

evidence.quote: A total of 15,480 participants underwent randomization. During a mean follow-up of 7.4 years

claims.text: There was no significant difference between the aspirin and placebo groups in the incidence of gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 [2.0%] vs 158 [2.0%]) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] vs 887 [11.5%]).

evidence.quote: There was no significant difference between the aspirin group and the placebo group in the incidence of gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 participants [2.0%] and 158 [2.0%], respectively) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] and 887 [11.5%]); long-term follow-up for these outcomes is planned.

claims.text: ASPREE enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 years or older (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) without cardiovascular disease, dementia or disability, randomly assigned to 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo.

evidence.quote: From 2010 through 2014, we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability. Participants were randomly assigned to receive 100 mg of enteric-coated aspirin or placebo.

claims.text: Of the 19,114 persons enrolled, 9525 were assigned to aspirin and 9589 to placebo, with a median follow-up of 4.7 years.

evidence.quote: Of the 19,114 persons who were enrolled in the trial, 9525 were assigned to receive aspirin and 9589 to receive placebo. After a median of 4.7 years of follow-up

claims.text: The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo.

evidence.quote: The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo.

claims.text: In ASPREE, the risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years with aspirin and 11.1 with placebo (HR 1.14; 95% CI 1.01-1.29), with cancer the major contributor to the higher mortality in the aspirin group.

evidence.quote: The risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.29). Cancer was the major contributor to the higher mortality in the aspirin group, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years.

claims.text: Cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% of participants in the aspirin group and 2.3% of those in the placebo group (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.10-1.56).

evidence.quote: Cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% of the participants in the aspirin group and in 2.3% of those in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.56).

claims.text: Higher all-cause mortality was observed among apparently healthy older adults who received daily aspirin than among those who received placebo and was attributed primarily to cancer-related death, a result described as unexpected and to be interpreted with caution.

evidence.quote: Higher all-cause mortality was observed among apparently healthy older adults who received daily aspirin than among those who received placebo and was attributed primarily to cancer-related death. In the context of previous studies, this result was unexpected and should be interpreted with caution.

claims.text: JPPP was a multicenter, open-label, randomized, parallel-group trial of 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia or diabetes mellitus, recruited at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007 and followed up for up to 6.5 years.

evidence.quote: The Japanese Primary Prevention Project (JPPP) was a multicenter, open-label, randomized, parallel-group trial. Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, and were followed up for up to 6.5 years, with last follow-up in May 2012.

claims.text: Patients were randomized 1:1 to enteric-coated aspirin 100 mg/d or no aspirin in addition to ongoing medications.

evidence.quote: Patients were randomized 1:1 to enteric-coated aspirin 100 mg/d or no aspirin in addition to ongoing medications.

claims.text: The study was terminated early by the data monitoring committee after a median follow-up of 5.02 years based on likely futility.

evidence.quote: The study was terminated early by the data monitoring committee after a median follow-up of 5.02 years (interquartile range, 4.55-5.33) based on likely futility.

lint.note: Direction of benefit differs by population: ASCEND found a significant reduction in serious vascular events in adults with diabetes (rate ratio 0.88), while ARRIVE (moderate risk), JPPP (older Japanese with risk factors) and ASPREE (older adults) found no significant reduction in their primary cardiovascular endpoints. The meta-analysis of 13 trials found a significant composite reduction overall.

ASPREE reports higher all-cause mortality with aspirin attributed primarily to cancer-related death, while ASCEND found no significant difference in all-cancer incidence; the ASPREE authors state the mortality result was unexpected and should be interpreted with caution.
